extraction_text: Uma, praised by Ganga, began to comprehensively explain female dharma.
Uma stated that female dharma is established at marriage, where a woman commits to following it with her husband.
Uma described a dharmic woman as virtuous, devoted solely to her husband's will, and treating him as a god.

A woman who listens to and serves her husband as if he were a deity, remains faithful and cheerful at all times, and gazes upon her husband's face with the same joy as upon her own son's face, behaves properly and follows rules, is considered a person who follows dharma.

A woman who pays attention to the duties of householder and mistress, happily performs these duties with her husband, follows her husband's will without improper thoughts, is considered a person who follows dharma.
Even if her husband speaks harshly or looks at her with anger, if she continues to smile at him, then this woman is truly devoted to her husband.
A woman with graceful appearance who, apart from her husband, does not look at the moon, sun, trees, or anything with a masculine name, is considered a person who follows dharma.
A woman who treats her husband the same as her own son, whether he is poor, sick, or exhausted from long journeys, is considered someone who can share merit with her husband.
A woman who restrains herself, is capable and intelligent, bears children, loves her husband as her own life, is considered someone who can share merit with her husband.
A woman who is humble, cheerful, and serves her husband wholeheartedly, is considered someone who can share merit with her husband.

A woman who concentrates all her feelings on her husband, while caring little for personal enjoyment, pleasure, prominence, or satisfaction of desires, is considered someone who can share merit with her husband.

A woman who complies with all requests from elders, rises at dawn, cleans the house inside and out with cow dung daily, maintains the household sacred fire, worships deities with flowers and offerings, serves food to deities, guests, and servants with her husband according to proper rules, watches them eat with satisfaction, then eats the remainder herself - such a woman can be said to have merged with dharma.
If a virtuous woman can satisfy her mother-in-law and father-in-law, and also serve her own mother and father diligently, then she is a person whose wealth is austerity.
A woman who regularly provides food to Brahmins who are weak, blind, helpless, or unfortunate, is considered someone who can share merit with her husband.

A woman who, despite her delicate body, undertakes heavy duties, constantly finds happiness in her husband's happiness, and keeps her thoughts focused on her husband, is considered someone who can share merit with her husband.
A woman who takes her husband's duties as her own, and whose life purpose is to assist her husband, is a happy person. For her, these are her austerities, her merit, and her eternal heaven.
Shiva's wife (Parvati) explains the duties of a wife according to dharma, emphasizing that the husband is her god, friend, and ultimate refuge.
Parvati states that a wife must obey her husband even in difficult circumstances, including doing things against dharma or life-threatening if he commands it.
Shiva (referred to as 'Lord of Gods' and 'Bhava') listens to Parvati's discourse, shows her deep respect, and dismisses the assembled audience including gods, rivers, Gandharvas, and Apsaras.
